newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Norwich Union, Tobacco risks.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Norwich Union, Tobacco risks.

text.p: UK mutual insurer Norwich Union is taking a brave step in allowing potential investors to look down its gullet. Unlike other demutualisations, NU is asking the City to cough up 1.75 billion stg in cash to fill the hole left in its life fund when the group is restructured.

Before the City does so, analysts will look deep into its mouth and may decide its teeth are too worn. The financial services industry is consolidating fast with banks and insurers uniting to meet the threat from the supermarkets. The Norwich may be one of Britain's largest life insurers, but there is a question mark over its preparedness to cope with the challenges it will face in its market over the next decade.

As Proteus has suggested before, the whole affair might be enlivened by a bit of bid speculation. But even here the Norwich may be found wanting. At 5.0 billion stg, it is a little too large to be an easy take-over target for some of the suitors who might see a fit.
The major tobacco manufacturers have for years united behind the party line that they do not insure against liabilities to smokers.

Their official reason was, of course, that smokers are clear thinking people warned of any potential risk. The real reason is twofold. Cigarette manufacturers don't want to create a 'pocket' of money which lawyers for alleged victims of smoking can target, and they don't want to do anything which the same lawyers can point to as an admission of guilt. Too many times before in other litigation cases, judges and juries have decided that by provisioning against liabilities the defendant had accepted its existence.

This was how Proteus saw things until Mr Paul Hodges, insurance specialist at Schroder Securities, arrived on the scene last week. Reports in the press indicate that Mr Hodges is on the verge of producing a note saying that in fact manufacturers such as BAT Industries have purchased much more insurance than they ever let on. The same newspapers also suggest that the tobacco firms are trying to dissuade him from publication.
So if any insurers or brokers among the readership of GINS can provide greater clarity on the situation, do please pick up the 'phone and give Reuters a call.
